summary: Defines terminology for the behaviors of NATs handling unicast UDP and sets requirements so applications like voice, video and online gaming work consistently through them. This is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: A NAT is like a receptionist who rewrites addresses on envelopes. This sets rules for how the receptionist should treat UDP mail so games and calls go through smoothly.

subtitle: What a NAT should do with UDP so that calls, video and games keep working through it.

tldr.problem: NATs behave very differently from one another, which makes it hard to predict whether voice, video and online gaming applications will work through any given NAT.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines common terminology for NAT mapping, filtering and related behaviors, then sets 14 requirements (REQ-1 to REQ-14) for unicast UDP, such as endpoint-independent mapping, hairpinning support and deterministic behavior.
tldr.outcome: A NAT that meets the MUST requirements is compliant, and one that also meets the RECOMMENDED ones is fully compliant. RFC 4787 is a Best Current Practice and has been updated by RFC 6888 and RFC 7857.

today: RFC 4787 is a Best Current Practice and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 6888 and RFC 7857.

sections.title: Why NAT Behavior Needs Requirements
sections.content:
Network Address Translators (NATs) cause significant problems for applications that carry IP addresses in their payload, including Voice over IP and online gaming. Many workarounds exist, including Application Level Gateways, STUN, Teredo and UDP relays, but UDP relays are generally seen as a solution of last resort. Meeting this RFC's requirements ensures that applications will not be forced to use a UDP relay.

The RFC notes that different NAT implementations vary widely in how they handle traffic, which makes behavior hard to predict. NAT vendors told the authors they would prefer NATs that are deterministic and do the least harm to applications. The goals are to define common terminology for NAT behavior and a set of requirements on specific behaviors.

The scope is narrow: Traditional NATs, from residential to enterprise, handling unicast UDP. Firewall behavior, directly signaled control of middleboxes, UDP relays and application aspects are out of scope. The RFC drops the old Full Cone, Restricted Cone, Port Restricted Cone and Symmetric labels from STUN because they proved inadequate, and describes individual behaviors instead.
sections.eli5: Every receptionist handles the mail a little differently, so nobody knows if their letters will arrive. This document says how a good receptionist should behave.

sections.title: Address and Port Mapping
sections.content:
When an internal endpoint opens an outgoing session, the NAT assigns an external IP address and port, called a mapping. The key question is when the NAT reuses that mapping for a new session from the same internal address and port (X:x) to a different external destination. The RFC defines three answers:

  • Endpoint-Independent Mapping: the mapping is reused for any external address and port.
  • Address-Dependent Mapping: reused only when the external IP address is the same, whatever the port.
  • Address and Port-Dependent Mapping: reused only when both the external address and port are the same.

REQ-1 says a NAT MUST have Endpoint-Independent Mapping, because UNSAF methods need it. Failing it forces the use of a UDP relay. The RFC stresses that mapping choice does not change a NAT's security properties, which depend on filtering.

Some NATs have a pool of external addresses. An Arbitrary pooling NAT may give one internal host several external addresses at once, which can break applications that use multiple ports, such as RTP and RTCP. REQ-2 therefore RECOMMENDS Paired pooling, where one internal address always maps to the same external address.
sections.eli5: When you send letters to different friends, the receptionist should always write the same return address on them. If the return address changes for each friend, nobody can write back reliably.

sections.title: Ports, Timers and Address Conflicts
sections.content:
Port assignment. Some NATs try to keep the internal port number (port preservation). Some always preserve it even on collision, which is called port overloading, and most applications fail with it. REQ-3 says a NAT MUST NOT use port overloading, and RECOMMENDS keeping the source port in the same range: 0-1023 stays within 0-1023, and 1024-65535 stays within 1024-65535. REQ-4 RECOMMENDS preserving port parity, so even ports map to even and odd to odd, which helps RTP and RTCP applications that follow RFC 3550. The RFC does not try to preserve the RTCP=RTP+1 contiguity rule.

Mapping refresh. The mapping timer is how long a mapping stays active without packets. REQ-5 says it MUST NOT expire in less than two minutes, though shorter timers are allowed for specific well-known destination ports (0-1023), and a default of five minutes or more is RECOMMENDED. REQ-6 says outbound packets MUST refresh the mapping. Inbound refresh is optional, and the RFC warns it may let an external attacker keep a mapping alive indefinitely.

Conflicting address spaces. If a NAT's external side uses an RFC 1918 private address, it may overlap with its internal network. REQ-7 says a NAT whose external interface can be configured dynamically MUST either pick a non-conflicting internal network or be able to translate traffic between all internal nodes and conflicting external nodes.
sections.eli5: The receptionist should not reuse a mailbox number for two people at once. She should also keep the return address valid for at least a couple of minutes after your last letter.

sections.title: Filtering and Hairpinning
sections.content:
Filtering decides which incoming packets the NAT lets through to an internal endpoint. With Endpoint-Independent Filtering, any external source may send to the mapped port once the internal host has sent anything out. With Address-Dependent Filtering, the internal host must first have sent to that external IP address. With Address and Port-Dependent Filtering, it must first have sent to that external address and port.

REQ-8 RECOMMENDS Endpoint-Independent Filtering if application transparency matters most, or Address-Dependent Filtering if stricter filtering matters most, and allows the choice to be configurable. The RFC admits that filtering independently of the external endpoint is less secure, but argues it works better for games and for ICE connectivity checks.

Hairpinning is when two hosts behind the same NAT talk to each other using their external addresses. The NAT receives a packet from X1 addressed to X2's external address and forwards it back inside to X2. REQ-9 says a NAT MUST support hairpinning, and the hairpinned packet MUST carry the external source IP address and port, not the internal one, since some applications reject packets from unexpected addresses.
sections.eli5: Filtering is the receptionist deciding whose letters to accept. Hairpinning is two people in the same building mailing each other through the front desk using the public address.

sections.title: ALGs, Determinism, ICMP and Fragments
sections.content:
Application Level Gateways (ALGs) rewrite application protocols such as SIP and can interfere with NAT traversal methods. REQ-10 says ALGs for UDP-based protocols SHOULD be turned off, and a NAT with ALGs should let the administrator enable or disable each separately.

A NAT that changes its mapping or filtering behavior without a configuration change, for example after a port conflict, is non-deterministic. REQ-11 says a NAT MUST be deterministic. Such NATs are hard to troubleshoot, and the RFC calls this behavior a root cause of much of the uncertainty about whether applications will work.

ICMP. REQ-12 says receipt of any ICMP message MUST NOT terminate the mapping. A NAT SHOULD NOT filter ICMP by source address by default, and SHOULD rewrite and forward ICMP messages. Blocking Destination Unreachable can interfere with Path MTU Discovery and traceroute.

Fragments. For outgoing packets, REQ-13 says if the DF bit is 1 the NAT MUST send back an ICMP "Fragmentation needed and DF set" message, and if DF is 0 it MUST fragment the packet. REQ-14 says a NAT MUST handle incoming fragments both in order and out of order, and its design MUST keep fragmentation-based denial of service from harming normal traffic.
sections.eli5: The receptionist should not secretly change her rules, should pass along "undeliverable" notices, and should be able to handle big parcels that arrive in pieces.

sections.title: The Requirement Checklist
sections.content:
Section 12 gathers REQ-1 to REQ-14 in one place. A NAT that supports all the MUST requirements is "compliant with this specification". A NAT that supports all requirements, including the RECOMMENDED ones, is "fully compliant with all the mandatory and recommended requirements".

The RFC adds a caution: applications normally do not know in advance whether a NAT conforms, so peer-to-peer media applications still need normal procedures such as ICE.
sections.eli5: There is a checklist of fourteen good-receptionist rules. Follow the must-do ones and you pass. Follow the should-do ones too and you get top marks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most requirements do not change the security properties of NATs, but a few do. Refreshing timers on outbound packets only (REQ-6) avoids letting an external attacker keep a mapping alive forever. Endpoint-independent mapping does not reduce security, because which packets cross the device is decided by filtering. Filtering on the external IP address only (REQ-8) can be argued to be less secure than filtering on address and port, but devices that filter on both still comply.

Non-deterministic NATs are risky because testing may suggest the NAT behaves as intended, while an attacker can create conditions under which it behaves differently. Accepting out-of-order fragments requires storing them, which can open a denial-of-service opportunity if done incorrectly, so implementers are pointed to RFC 3128 and RFC 1858.

The RFC also has an IAB Considerations section. It says the document is not itself an UNSAF proposal and does not reduce the overall brittleness of NATs, but hopes to reduce some of the more outrageous NAT behaviors.
sections.eli5: The main danger is a receptionist who acts differently when you are not watching, or who keeps a door open too long. So the rules ask her to be predictable and to close doors on time.
